query: For nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and initially crystallized as a solid solution, what governs whether structural and chemical stability is maintained across catalytic and thermoelectric operating ranges of 473–1923 K? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled comparison, predict observations relative to the initial baseline, define the conditions under which the prediction should hold, identify supporting evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In equimolar multimetallic nanoparticles, the maintenance of a single-phase solid solution over catalytic and thermoelectric operating ranges up to 1923 K is governed by the interplay between high configurational entropy and sluggish atomic diffusion. When the high configurational entropy dominates and diffusion kinetics remain slow, the nanoparticles preserve their uniform structure. However, if thermal energy or reactive environments effectively lower the kinetic barriers, localized elemental segregation and secondary phase formation will occur.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanoparticles composed of five or more metals at near-equiatomic ratios, crystallized as a single-phase solid solution.
generation.intervention: Perform in situ high-temperature experiments (e.g., using synchrotron X-ray diffraction, high-resolution electron microscopy, and elemental mapping) on the nanoparticles under controlled catalytic and thermoelectric environments across 473–1923 K.
generation.conditions: Measurements conducted in inert or application-similar reactive atmospheres with controlled heating rates; comparisons between conditions where the diffusion barriers are expected to remain intact versus those where they may be compromised (e.g., extended exposure or reactive gases).
generation.structural_mediator: Real-time tracking of crystal structure, grain boundaries, and elemental distribution to detect any onset of phase changes or segregation.
generation.mechanism: High configurational entropy thermodynamically favors the single-phase solid solution, while the inherent lattice distortions and severe atomic size mismatches create high diffusion barriers (sluggish kinetics) that inhibit atomic rearrangement and segregation. Once the thermal energy becomes sufficient to overcome these kinetic barriers, the structure may decompose locally.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under controlled inert conditions, the nanoparticles will maintain their single-phase structure with uniform elemental distribution up to 1923 K. In contrast, under conditions that lower kinetic barriers (e.g., reactive environments or extended high-temperature annealing), early signs of elemental segregation and/or formation of secondary phases will be observed relative to the initial state.
generation.baseline: The as-synthesized uniform single-phase solid solution state as confirmed by initial structural and compositional measurements at room temperature.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis should hold provided that the sample environment does not introduce unexpected reactive species or non-equilibrium conditions that independently promote diffusion; deviations observed below 1923 K or under minimal thermal driving force would falsify the hypothesis.
generation.uncertainty: The exact temperature threshold or time scale over which kinetic barriers are overcome is uncertain and may depend on the specific elemental combinations and the detailed nature of the operating environment.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a series of in situ high-temperature experiments on the quinary (or multinary) nanoparticles using simultaneous synchrotron X-ray diffraction, high-resolution electron microscopy, and elemental mapping. Divide the experiments into two groups: one in an inert atmosphere and another in a mildly reactive (catalytic) environment. Incrementally increase the temperature from 473 K to 1923 K while holding at each temperature for sufficient time to allow diffusion.
measurements: Crystal phase (via XRD) to detect any phase transformation or lattice parameter changes.
Elemental distribution mapping (via EDS or similar) to detect segregation or compositional fluctuations.
Grain size and morphology changes (via high-resolution electron microscopy).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If significant elemental segregation or secondary phase formation is observed in the inert environment at temperatures well below 1923 K (or without an expected reduction in kinetic barriers), or if the single-phase structure is maintained regardless of conditions known to lower diffusion barriers, then the mechanism attributing stability to the interplay of configurational entropy and sluggish kinetics is falsified.

The stability of the MEA-NPs is critical for their practical application at elevated temperatures. We, therefore, performed an in situ stability test in the electron microscope from room temperature up to 873 K, annealing the NPs at each test point for at least 30 min. As shown in Fig. 4A, the ultrafine Ru-5 MEA-NPs maintain their uniform dispersion throughout the in situ tests up to 873 K and demonstrate superior size stability after high-temperature annealing. In addition, the NPs are still in a homogeneous alloy structure without elemental segregation or phase separation (Fig. 4B), showing their structural stability. Note that the Co and Ni after annealing are slightly less than the nominal composition, which is likely due to metal evaporation at high temperature in the microscope vacuum. We also confirmed the alloy structure macroscopically by powder and synchrotron x-ray diffraction, showing a single-phase fcc structure with a fitted lattice constant of 3.673 Å (fig. S3, B and C).

decision.trend: Early studies on CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloys revealed temperature-driven phase transformations (e.g., fcc-to-hcp polymorphisms) under thermal or pressure stresses. Subsequent work demonstrated single-phase quinary and multinary nanoparticles (e.g., CoMoFeNiCu, PtPdCoCuNi) for catalytic applications, establishing their potential for stable performance. High-throughput computational mapping then identified broader compositional windows in equimolar quinary alloys with robust solid-solution formation. More recent studies probed dissolution phenomena and formation pathways using in situ techniques, clarifying that kinetic factors (e.g., surface segregation) can undermine the high configurational entropy benefits under reactive conditions. Although these strategies have extended operational temperatures, the interplay of core–shell segregation, transient phase formation, and the reliability of entropic stabilization across broad catalytic and thermoelectric windows remains incompletely understood.
decision.unsolved: It is still unclear how competing thermodynamic (entropic stabilization versus elemental incompatibilities) and kinetic factors (segregation, surface diffusion, phase transformations) balance to maintain or disrupt single-phase structural and chemical uniformity from intermediate (∼473 K) to very high (≥1500 K) temperatures under reaction conditions. Understanding the mechanism driving high-temperature atomic and structural stability, and correlating it with potential degradative pathways (e.g., segregation, particle coalescence, partial phase separation), remains an open challenge.
decision.lever: Employ multi-modal in situ characterization—simultaneous high-temperature synchrotron X-ray diffraction, high-resolution electron microscopy, and elemental mapping—on the same quinary nanoparticles operating under simulated catalytic or thermoelectric conditions from 473‒1923 K to track real-time changes in crystal structure, local composition, and surface segregation behavior.
decision.why: This approach systematically addresses the need to observe how restructuring, diffusion, and phase transformations occur across a broad thermal range under application-relevant environments, directly testing the hypothesis that high configurational entropy can stabilize a single solid solution structure against thermal and chemical perturbations up to 1923 K. By detecting any emergent secondary phases or preferential depletion/enrichment of certain elements at surfaces or grain boundaries, this study would clarify the principal mechanisms governing the nanoparticles’ structural and chemical stability, and falsify the hypothesis if significant deviations from the single-phase, near-equiatomic state are observed within the targeted temperature range.
